ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Purchase of pipes by GAIL 
*301.   SHRIRAJU PARMAR:†† 
SHRIR. K.ANAND: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Gas Authority of India Limited (GAIL) has invited 
tenders for purchase of expensive longitudinally-welded pipes for laying down 
its Dahej-Vijaipur pipeline project; 
(b) if so, what are the details in this regard and whether GAIL is losing 
more than Rs. 450 crores on the purchase of these pipes ignoring the advice of its 
authorised Belgium-based Engineers Consultant; and 
(c) whether Government would probe the matter and if not, the reasons 
therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) GAIL (India) Limited ( GAIL) has reported that they have 
procured pipes for their Dahej-Vijaipur Pipeline Project (DVPL) through 
international competitive bidding wherein technically the best available 
^material at most competitive prices has been procured. The selection of 
vendors for procurement of pipelines has been done by GAIL keeping in view 
the pipeline requirement of the project and as per the technical advice of their 
consultants M/s Engineers India Limite d. Tractebel Engin eering, Belgium, 
who are consultants to GAIL for their upcoming 
†† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Raju Parmar. 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2003] 
Dahej-Uran Pipeline Project, has also recommended Longitudinally 
Submerged Arc Welded (LSAW) Pipes onl y as against the other alternative 
of Helically Submerged Arc Welded (HSAW) Pipes. GAIL has denied that it 
has spent an extra amount of Rs. 450 crore in procuring pipes for its gas pipeline 
project. Based on safety and economic considerations, GAIL has to take a 
view on specifications of material to be procured for gas pipelines. 
Government will issue appropriate directions if considered necessary. 
SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Mr. Chairman , Sir, the American Petroleum 
Institute has specified broad usage of steel pipes for this kind of pipeline 
projects. If so, whether this Institute was consulted before the purchase of 
expensive pipes which don't conform to the basic specification laid down by 
the American Petroleum Institute. 
SHRI RAM NAIK: Sir, whatever sp ecifications are given by that 
American Institute, they have been followed. We have appointed Engineers 
India Limited as our Consultant, and all procedures and formalsties are 
followed. Sir, on this occasion, I would like to inform the House—and it is a 
good news—that the first LNG terminal of the country for the import of LNG is 
getting ready and would be completed in the first week of January. The new 
gas, LNG, will come to India by the end of January and, thereafter, many 
problem of having gas shortage would be over. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: There would be no need to put questions further! 
SHRI RAM NAIK: Sir, the follow-up questions can be put. 
SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Sir, the Steel Authority of India and other 
leading indigenous manufacturers are also manufacturing similar types of 
steel pipes and their rates are around $ 585 per metric tonne. I would like to 
know the reasons for not exploring the possibility of procuring these pipes 
from SAIL or local manufacturers. I would also like to know whether the 
Government would consider procuring these pipes from SAIL or local 
manufacturers for their future requirements. 
SHRI RAM NAIK: Sir, the Consultant advised the use of LSAW 
(Longitudinally Submerged Arc Welded Pipes) and that is being done. 
2

Now the SAIL is manufacturing different types of tubes. All the orders which 
have been given now, have luckily gone to the Indian manufacturers only and the 
the comparision of the price which th e hon. Member has done-probably, he 
has taken the figure from Chinese. When the Chinese pipes woule be brought 
here, we have to add our import duty and other transport charges added, we have 
seen that, practically, the rate is at par. So, there is no high rate at which this is 
purchased.

*302. SHRI RUMANDLA RAAMACHANDRAYYA: Will the Minister 
of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government of Andhra Pradesh has entered into an 
agreement with the Austrian Government for utilisation of Godavari water in 
hydel and irrigation projects; 
(b) whether water going waste and flowing into Bay of Bengal will be 
utilised with the implementation of this agreement; and 
 
(c) by when the work on the proposed projects is likely to be 
f commenced?

SETHI): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement

Memorandum of Undersanding (MoU) with the Government of Austria for 
exploring the possibility of widening cooperation in the development of 
Irrigation, Hydroelectric po wer, Health and Infrastru cture related projects

Pradesh and the Austrian Embassy

(c) The proposal in respect of Godavari Lift Irrigation Scheme and 
Pulichintala Project from the Government of Andhra Pradesh' for

Assistance to Assam from Social Security Fund 
*303. SHRI DWIJENDR A NATH SHARMAH: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have released financial assistance to Assam from 
Social Security Fund; 
(b) if so, the details of assistance re leased to the State during the last 
three years; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): (a) No, 
Sir. 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) Because, there is no such fund that is administered by the 
Government of India. 
SHRI DWIJENDRA NATH SHARMAH: Sir, there are a lot of killings by 
the extremist organizations in the country, including Assam. In most cases, it 
has been observed that th e head of the family dies and the family becomes 
helpless. May I know from the hon. Minister whether there is any such fund 
by which such families, where the head of the family dies, could be 
rehabilitated, and be given some sort of social security through financial help? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, as I shared with the hon. Member in my 
reply to the original question, there is no such fund that is administered by the 
Ministry of Finance. However, the Ministry of Social Welfare does have a 
National Social Assistance Programme, as also a National Family Benefit 
Scheme. If the hon. wants to have greater details about these programmes or 
schemes, the right Ministry, from which he should enquire, is the Ministry of 
Social Welfare. 
SHRI DWIJENDRA NATH SHARMAH: Sir, this is not connected only 
with the killings by the extremists, but there are a lot of people who are socially 
insecure and goes out of the social mainstream. Particularly, the people like the 
drug addicts, street children, etc. do not have any 
6 

[23 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
social security. Let us try to understand that; and a chance should be given to 
them to join the mainstream of the society. They need some sort of assistance 
through which they can start their life. I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister whether the Government has any such proposal. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, what the hon. Member is trying to say, 
in the context of Assam an d the North-East, is that misled youth are to be 
drawn back into the mainstream, and whether the Ministry of Finance have a 
scheme for encouraging that process. The State Government is involved in this, 
there are other Ministries which are involved in this. Directly, the Ministry of 
Finance does not have this responsibility. 
SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN: Sir, the hon. Minister has said that no such 
fund is administered by the Government of India. What is the difficulty in 
providing for such a fund? There is a lot of demand from the destitute people.

want of money, and they are in dire need of the Government's help. So, what 
is the difficulty in setting up such a fund to help them? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, I have to repeat what I said earlier that there 
is no difficulty in providing for a fund. There is already a fund, which is called 
the National Social Assistance Progra mme, and there is the National Family 
Pension Scheme. They are being administered by the Ministry of Social 
Welfare. The Finance Ministry's role comes in providing budgetary allocation to 
the Ministry of Social Welfare. They deal with two the Schemes of Old Age 
Pension and Family Benefit, etc., and the State Governments deal with subject. 
The Ministry of Finance is not a Social Welfare Ministry. The Ministry of 
Finance does provide assistance to the Ministry of Social Welfare, but we don't 
directly deal with the subject. 
Storage capacity of reservoirs 
*304. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the storage capacity of major reservoirs of the 
country has come down drastrically due to excessive silting; 
(b) if so, the details of the storage capacity of various reservoirs at the 
time of inception and now with special reference to Andhra Pradesh; 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2003] 
(c) whether there is any proposal to dredge the reservoirs; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RE SOURCES (SHRIARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Silting of reservoir is a natural process and provision is made at the 
planning stage itself for accumulation of sediment in reservoirs. The sediment 
flows accumulate in the dead storage provided for the purpose and thus the 
sediment deposition, in general, do not affect the efficacy of the project during 
the planned life of the reservoir. The studies on Silting of Reservoirs in India have 
indicated that while in some cases the rates of actual sedimentation are slightly 
less than that assumed at the time of planning, in other cases it is on higher 
side. 
(b) The details in respect of reservoirs including those in Andhra 
Pradesh where "Capacity Survey" have been conducted are given in the 
statement-1 (See below) 
(c) There is no proposal at present under consideration of the 
Government of India for dredging of the reservoirs. 
(d) Does not arise.

SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir it is not as if the 100 billion dollars are 
lying in a drawer, which can be pulled out and the money utilised for 
purchase of groceries of things like that. This is a national asset. The reserves 
have been built up over a period of time. The reserves, certainly, lend to my 
conviction a sense of much greater confidence within the country and the 
economic system. It enables our corporates to borrow better abroad. 
So far as the utilisation is concerned, on a medium-term basis, I would 
like to share with the hon. Member a longer picture because I see a considerable 
growth coming through the import bill requirements of the country, and when 
the import bill begings to go up, there will be a great deal of demand on our 
reserves. When that happens, then, there will be a draw-down. I don't believe that 
we have reached some kind of a plateau. Now, that India's reserves have 
reached where they have, it is my conviction again that they will continue to go. 
We have utilised our reserves in the past one year to pre-pay some of the high-cost 
debts. We have prepaid, Sir, as you know and as the hon. Members know very 
well almost 7 billion dollars. Despite the early repayment of 7 billion dollars, 
we have reached the figures that we have. Therefore, we will continue to pre-pay 
others. The Government of India has also initiated steps whereby we are no 
longer taking grants or assistance which we were earlier taking in very small 
denominations from a variety of countries, which stood by India in time of 
need. But we have now said this is , perhaps better utilised, if channelled 
either to other countries or through non-governmental organisations. We have 
also simultaneously, initiated steps whereby the Government of India now, in 
fact, grants loans and grants to some of the least developed countries as also 
others. So, it is serving many purposes, economic, commercial, psychological as 
also diplomatic.

were, converted into some kind of criminals as we would hide notes in our 
suitcases when travelling abroad so that they could be converted. That phase is 
over. The citizen can take monies abroad. The citizen can now purchase on 
credit cards while in India. The former Governor of Reserve Bank of India, who 
is currently with us as one of our distinguished Members, has done a lot in this 
regard. It is quite often cited that so far as the flow is concerned, there is no 
restriction on flow of money, but on the total convertibility of currency, many 
other factors come in-for example, the fisc al deficit state, so also the inflation 
state. And, there is a route map that the former Deputy Governor of Reserve Bank of 
India, Mr. Tarapore, had suggested to the country. So long as we are not able to 
combine fiscal and inflation at a level which is comfortable for us, I don't think 
there should be any anxiety about the full convertibility, b ecause benefits are 
available in almost near totality.

(a) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reported that out of 88 proposals for 
opening new Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) in the country, the Screening 
Committee constituted by RBI has recommended approval for only two 
proposals during 2002-03. 
(b) Urban co-operative banking sector in some areas was facing a certain 
level of criris on account of irregularities committed by a few UCBs which led to 
substantial losses. RBI was, therefore,  required to initiate specific regulatory 
and supervisory measures to address bank specific problems and to avoid the 
recurrence of irregularities.

in 2002-03, details the measures and other regulatory initiatives taken by the 
RBI during the year. RBI has set up a Committee of experts to screen proposals 
for new UCBs. The Committee takes into account the policy environment of the 
concerned State, track record and integrity of the promoters, requirements under 
prudential norms and the state of urban banking in the concerned State. The 
Committee has not recommended approval for the remaining proposals for

Transfer of Red Fort to ASI 
*306. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of TOURISM AND 
CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Army has already transferred portions of the 
Red Fort to the Archaeological Survey of India; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the complete charge would be handed over to 
the Archaeological Survey of India very soon; and 
(c) if so, what steps have been taken by Government to conserve and 
restore the past glory oTthe Red Fort? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI JAGMOHAN): 
(a) to (c) On December 22,2003 the Ministry of Defence/Army Headquarters have 
transferred the entire Red Fort monument to the Ministry of Tourism and 
Culture/Archaeological Survey of India. Previously, only about 30 percent of the Red 
Fort area was with the Archaeological Survey of India/Ministry of Tourism and 
Culture. 
39 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2003] 
A number of steps for conservation and restoration of the Red Fort have already 
been taken in the area which was previously in the possession of the Archaeological 
Survey of India and the remaining measures are in hand. 
The steps already taken include: 
1. A nauseating slum, known as 'Chor Bazaar', and an area with open 
urinals and closed drains, has been replaced by an enchanting park 
which stretches from the northen extremity of the Fort to the area 
fronting Raj Ghat. 
2. Similar treatment has been accorded to the vast uneven and uncared 
For area on Chandni Chowk side which has been converted into a 
beautiful national park—August 15 Park. 
3. The entire surface of the Fort walls—21,219 square metres—has been 
throughly washed and chemically cleaned. 
4. The 1.7 kilometre long moat w ith massive slush accumulated over 
the years has been cleared. About 23,000 cubic metres of debris, with 
a load of 3,500 trucks, has been lifted from it. 
5. About 2,200 square metres of pathways which were of flag stones and 
were subsequently damaged and replaced by 'morram', have been relaid in 
accordance with the original design. The shell plaster on the walls of 
Mumtaz Mahal, Rang Mahal, Hamma, which had peeled off, has been 
refixed. 
6. All the 23 red sandstone Ja//-windows, which had broken, have been 
remade and refixed. 
7. Diwan-I-Khas, Khas Mahal, Naubat-Khana, Tehkhana, too, have been 
restored to their old glory. 
8. The old underground passage to the Yamuna River Front, under the 
Musammam Burj, has been cleared and opened on the King Road side. 
9. A special treatment has been accorded to a virtually unknown baoli— 
step-well—which hides a small but an inspiring part of history of our 
freedom struggle. 
40 

[23 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
10. A new underground Ticket House' has also been constructed and 'Light 
and Sound Show' upgraded. 
The area (70 per cent) which was transferred yesterday by the Ministry of 
Defence/Army Headquarters to the Ministry of Tourism and Culture/ 
Archaeological Survey of India, would be planned for taking proper 
conservation and restoration measures. For undertaking necessary work in this 
regard, a high-level Advisory Committee has.been constituted and further action 
in the matter is in hand.

safeguarding genuine investors' interests particularly small investors? 
"THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) The Securities And Exchange 
Board of India (SEBI) regulates insider trading through SEBI (Prohibition Of 
Insider Trading) Regulations, 1992. R ecent measures taken to curb insider 
trading practices are: 
1. The SEBI Amendment Act, 2002 included specific provision 
prohibiting insider trading and substantially increasing the penalty which can be 
imposed for insider traditing to Rs. 25 crore or three times the amount of 
profits made, whichever is higher.

trading, the SEBI (Insider Trading) Amendment Regulations, 2002 provided 
for a model code of conduct to be followed by companies and SEBI registered 
intermediaries, and a code of corporate disclosure practices to be followed by 
listed companies. 
3. For detection of insider trading, surveillance mechanisms have been 
put in place by SEBI and stock exchanges. SEBI has further enhanced its 
surveillance through a regular system of weekly surveillance meetings with 
major stock exchanges and depositories to provide a platform for exchange of 
views on areas of emerging concerns and to consider pre-emptive actions and 
discuss general surveillance issues.

Higher interest rate by SBI 
2252. SHRI MURLI DEORA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether a Consortium of Banks led by SBI have been appropriating 
around 6 per cent of the budgeted provision for food subsidy by charging an 
interest of Rs. 10.95 per cent for food credit from Food Corporation of India 
while these banks are lending to Government at the rate of 4.5 per cent; 
(b) if so, the reasons for this anomaly; and 
(c) whether Government ars set to approve a bond flotation from 
theFCI in the debt market and if so , the details thereof and by when the 
proposal is likely to be approved? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
ANANDRAO VI THOBAADSUL): (a) and (b) Food Corporation of India 
(FCI) is the main agency for implem enting the Food Procurement and Public 
Distribution Policy of the Government of India. The mechanism for financing 
these operations is through the consortium of Banks and the rate of interest 
charged by the consortium of Banks is determined on the basis of average 
prime lending rates of the five largest Banks in the consortium. Currently rate 
of interest charged 10.95%. Food credit is also the first charge on the lendable 
resources of Commercial Banks and is not credit extended on pure 
commercial considerations. Bank's subscription to Government bonds is 
partly due to statutory stipulation of SLR and Banks have to keep a part of 
their assets in SLR while competing for the same bonds with other 
institutions. Banks do not lend to the Government directly but Banks 
subscribe to the bonds floated by Government periodically. Being sovereign 
paper the rates are not strictly comparable with commercial rates. 
(c) Discussions on the proposal to float bonds by Food Corporation of 
India are inconclusive at this stage.

offence, Rs. 50,000 and recovery of differential in retail selling price of 
domestic & commercial LPG for 2nd offence, and termination for 3rd 
offence, against the distributor is imposed.

supply domestic cylinders  for commercial purpose.  The officials of OMCs

frontier areas, as also exploration in the deeper layers of the producing fields. 
(iv) Faster development of newly discovered fields and stepping up of use 
of new technologies for seismic surveys, workover, simulation operations, 
drilling of wells, etc., in producing areas. 
(c) and (d) Seismic surveys are being conducted by the National Oil 
Companies namely, ONGC and Oil India Ltd. (OIL) as well as Private 
Companies/Joint Ventures in their allotted areas located in the States of Assam, 
Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Mizoram, 
Rajasthan, Tamilnadu, Tripura, and Uttar Pradesh as also in the offshore areas. 
The Seismic survey data, after processing and interpretation, provide 
information only about the presence of structures/leads and prospects. 
Presence or otherwise of hydrocarbons is known only after exploratory 
drilling.

[23 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI 
JAGMOHAN): (a) to (c) In a public Interest Litigation filed in the Supreme Court, a 
few faults have been alleged about the nature of conservation and restoration work 
undertaken by the Archaeological Survey of India in the Red Fort, the Archaeological Survey 
of India/Government of India have refuted the alleged faults in a sworn affidavit and 
submitted that the entire restoration/conservation work has been carried out by the 
Archaeological Survey of India in accordance with the provisions of the Conservation 
Manual and well established norms as well as valid documents and old records which 
are in the archives of the Archaeological Survey in India. 
On December 22,2003, the Ministry of Defence/Army Headquarters have transferred 
the entire Red Fort monument to the Ministry of Tourism and Culture/Archaeological 
Survey of India. Previously, only about 30 per cent of the Red Fort area was with the 
Archaeological Survey of India/ Ministry of Tourism and Culture. 
A number of steps for conservation and restoration of the Red Fort have already 
been taken in the area which was previously in the possession of the Archaeological 
Survey of India and the remaining measures are in hand. 
The steps already taken include: 
1. A nauseating slum, known as "Chor Bazaar" and an area with open 
urinals and clogged drains, has been replaced by an enchanting park 
which stretches from the northern extremity of the Fort to the area 
fronting Raj Ghat.

2309.  SHRIMATISAVITASHARDA: 
SHRI LALIT BHAI MEHTA: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the per capita availability of water in cubic meters, State-wise, 
in the country; 
(b) what is the international standard of per capita water to be available to an 
individual; 
(c) whether it is a fact that because of Sardar Sarovar Narmada Dam 
Project only, the increased per capita water supply of 150 cubic meters would 
be available to Gujarat; and 
(d) in what manner the shortfall of water availability is to be met in the 
country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATIBIJOYACHAKRAVARTY): (a) The per capita 
availability of water is not assessed State-wise. It is assessed river basin-wise. 
River basin-wise water availability and per capita availability of water is given at 
Annex. 
(b) As per international criterion, the annual per capita availability of water 
of less than 1000 cubic metre is considered as scarcity condition. 
(c) As per Narmada Water Disputes  Tribunal Award, the annual 
utilizable quantum of Narmada water (at 75% dependability), which will 
become available to Gujarat from the Sardar Sarovar Narmada Project, is 
11,101.32 million cubic metres (9.00 million acre feet (MAF). Thus the 
utilization of water will increase by about 11,101.32 cubic metre and by 
dividing the same with the total population of Gujarat, the per capita increase 
in utilization of water as a result of construction of Sardar Sarovar Narmada Dam 
works out to be of the order of 219.4 cubic metre. 
(d) To meet the projected water requirements, a live storage capacity of 177 
billion cubic metre (BCM) has already been created. An additional live storage 
capacity of 75 BCM will be created on completion of the ongoing projects, 
Besides, proposals for additional projects are also under formulation consideration 
for creation of storage capacity of 132 BCM. To accelerate creation of irrigation 
potential by early completion of ongoing schemes, Government of India has 
launched Accelerated Irrigation Benefits 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2003] 
Programme (AIBP). Government of India is also promoting rainwater 
harvesting through Watershed Management Programme, artificial recharge of 
ground water and roof-top rainwater harvesting under the sector reform project of 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply Progr amme of the Ministry of Rural 
Development, for which technical and financial assistance is provided to the State 
Governments and other implementing agencies. Central Ground Water Board 
has also taken up a Central Sector Scheme on "Studies of Recharge to Ground 
Water" on pilot basis. For meeting future requirements of water, as a long 
term measure, a National Perspective Plan for water resources development has 
been formulated by the Ministry which has two components namely Peninsular

Water supply for agriculture 
2316. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 80 per cent of the total water supply in our 
country is used for agriculture against 70 per cent in the world; 
(b) whether considering the large amount of water used for irrigation as 
India's irrigated area is more than 20 per cent of the world area under irrigation, 
there is an urgent need for conservati on and efficient use of these resources; 
and 
(c) if so, what are Government's reaction thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) About 83% of 
utilizable water in the country is being used for irrigation at present against 69% in 
the world. 
(b) and (c) Yes, there is an urgent need for conservation and efficient use of 
water resources. The National Water Policy adopted by the Government of 
India in 2002 stipulates that "efficiency of utilisation in all the diverse uses of 
water should be optimized and an awareness of water as a scarce resource should 
be fostered. Conservation consciousness should be promoted through 
education, regulation, incentives and disincentives. The resources should be 
conserved and the availability augmented by maximizing retention, eliminating 
pollution and minimising 
192 

[23 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
losses. For this, measures like selective lining in the conveyance system, 
modernisation and rehabilitation of existing systems including tanks, 
recycling and re-use of treated effluents and adoption of traditional techniques 
like mulching or pitcher irrigation and new techniques like drip and sprinkler 
may be promoted, wherever feasible." The Prime Minister has also made an 
appeal to the Nation for making water conservation a National Mission. The 
Government encourages various measures for conservation and efficient use 
of water. 
Water consumption in Thermal Power Plants 
2317. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as per a recenty study on water resources in our 
country, Thermal Power Plants consume 87.87 per cent of the water consumed by 
the industry; 
(b) whether it is fact that this water is consumed inefficiently and the 
consumption per power unit is 8 times that of international standards and costs a 
pittance; and 
(c) if so, what are Government's reaction thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) As per 
assessment made by the "National Commission for Integrated Water 
Resources Development Plan", the consumption of water by Power Plants is about 
30% of that by the industries. 
(b) Thermal Power Stations consume relatively higher amount of water 
for condensation of steam and for cooling of auxiliaries and ash disposal. 
Most of the old power stations have a once through cooling system where 
though large cooling water is drawn from the water body and most of it is 
discharged back to the water body after circulation through the cooling system. As 
such, a very small quantity of 2-3% of the total water drawn is actually 
consumed. Due to ambient conditions of higher temperature, heat rejection in 
stations in India is higher which increases the cooling water requirement. 
193 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2003] 
(c) Following steps are taken to conserve water used in power 
stations:— 
(i) As per Ministry of Environment and Forests, it is necessasry for all 
new stations to provide closed cycle cooling water systems where 
only a very small quantity of cooling water (2-3%) of the once-
through system is drawn from the water body for make up 
purposes. Zero discharge concept is also being adopted wherever 
possible. 
(ii) To reduce consumption of water for ash disposal, ash water 
recycling system is being provided in all the power stations. 
Further the utilisation of ash has been made mandatory and the 
utilities have been directed by Ministry of Environment and 
Forests to achieve 100% ash utilisation within a stipulated period. 
This will reduce the consumption of water in thermal power 
stations for ash disposal. 
(iii) In case of coastal locations, seawater is used for condenser 
cooling. 
(iv) Further, new techonology means such as dry cooling of 
condensers etc. are being considered for optimizing cooling water 
requirements of Thermal Power Stations.

SHORT DURATION DISCUSSION— 
THE FAKE STAMP PAPERS SCAM IN THE COUNTRY INVOLVING 
SEVERAL THOUSAND CRORES OF RUPEES 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): On the question 
of stamp papers discussion, I have to very briefly share with the hon. Members 
that so far as the Ministry of Finance is  concerned, we administer, the Ministry 
of Finance administer the Indian Security Press, Nashik and the Security 
Printing Press, Hyderabad These two are the units that supply judicial, non-
jodicial and other stamp papers to the States and the Union Territories. The 
administering is on the authority of an Act— The Indian Stamp Act, 1899. States 
can have their own Stamp Act and some States like Karnataka, Maharashtra, 
Gujarat, etc., do have their own Stamp Acts. All revenues from stamp duties 
accrue to the State Governments who decide who is to be licensed as a stamp 
vendor, method of collection, record keeping, accounting and all other such such 
related aspects. Now, I wish to share with the hon. Members the chronology of 
events of the entire stamp paper matter. One is that on 5th of March, 1998, 
sale of a perforating machine to an enterprise called the Unique Enterprises, 
took place. This is a routine exercise which is undertaken when machines get 
old; they are replaced with new ones and the old machines are sold through 
an auction, but the requirement, the entire conditionalities of sale require that 
they be destroyed, the cipher be destroyed, the blocks be destroyed and thereafter, 
the machine be disposed of. So, as I said on 5th March, 1998, before the 
National Democratic 
371 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2003] 
Alliance Government was shown in office, one of the machines was sold. On 1st 
April, 1998, soon after the National Democratic Alliance was sworn in, two more 
perforating machines were sold to the Unique Enterprises. About a year-and-a-
half later, in November of 2000, first reports of forgery, because of the Co-
ordinating Committee meetings, appeared in stamp papers and there was, at 
that stage, in November, 2000, no indi cation of any organised racket or 
involvement of any of the Security Press officials. In July of 2002—it is correct and I 
said so in the other House also. An hon. Members has raised this query.—I was 
given the charge of the Ministry of Finance. And, I then received, within days of 
my getting the charge, a letter from Chief Minister of Karnataka who suggested 
in the letter that some foolproof measur es should be introduced in the Security 
Press, also suggesting that there existed or there could be alleging that there 
existed some liaison or nexus between the ISP personnel and this entire matter. 
However, in that letter, no ISP personnel had been named. Immediately 
thereafter, I, of course, had acknowledged the letter, but I was absolutely new to 
the Ministry and I hadn't any knowledge or any investigation hadn't taken place. 
So, what we did was that we made an im mediate reference of this issue to the 
Intelligence Bureau to maintain surveillance, additional surveillance, because the 
machinery that we had at our disposal in the Ministry of Finance was not adequate 
to do so. So, Intelligence Bureau was requested to maintain additional surveillance 
over the ISP and the CNP at Nashik. In August of 2002, the Ministry of Finance 
alerted all security agencies and the surveillance over the two Presses was 
further tightened. In October, 2002, the CISF, took some time because we made a 
request, the requisition to CISF. My in vestigations had es tablished that the 
security arrangements were not very satisfactory, even the para-military 
security. So, the CISF replaced in October, 2002, the Departmental security at 
Nashik. In the December of 2002, further streamlining of system was requested 
and in January, 2003,1 received letter again from the Chief Ministry of Karnataka, as 
also from Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh recommending certain additional 
features in the nonjudicial stamp papers. We then convened a meeting at Nashik 
with security agencies to review all the security arrangement all over again. In 
February of 2003, the Working Group recommendations on new features of the non-
judicial stamp papers were approved and one of the Security Press officials was 
suspended. In March, 2003,1 wrote, at length, to the Chief Ministers both of 
Karnataka and of Andhra Pradesh and again a further review of 
372 

[23 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
the security arrangements. Likewise in  April, 2003, the General Manager of 
Nashik Press was transferred whereafter all Chief Secretaries were advised to 
report, to ensure vigilance regarding any false or fake stamp papers and to verify 
stock and vendors. In July, 2003, the Home Secretary— by then we had requested 
the Home Ministry also—held a meeting with the State Chief Secretaries and 
the Directors General of Police, and the General Manager of the Security Press 
was suspended alongwith two others, three Deputy General Managers were 
transferred away from Nashik. In August, I recommended the dismissal of the 
General Manager of ISP, and, this was sent to the Department of Personnel and 
Training. In October this year, the production with new features of the non-judicial 
stamp papers started, and, we began to supply this new feature stamp papers to 
Andhra, and, all States would hereafter be covered by July of next year. 
More officials have been suspended at Nashik. But as far as CBI is 
concerned, the CBI is at present investigating seven cases relating to the stamp 
paper matter pertaining to the States, namely, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Delhi 
and Andhra Pradesh. The CBI has been given the go-ahead by the Ministry of 
Finance to take suitable action against the Security Press officials, and, the 
Government of India is determined because it is a very important issue that all 
guilty are brought to book and punished without delay. The Government of India 
is also filing a representation so that all cases having inter-state ramifications 
about fake stamp papers are transferred to the CBI, and, requesting the State 
Police of Maharashtra and Karnataka to share all their documents and material 
collected during their investigations with the Central Bureau of Investigation so as to 
enable the CBI to investigate the full implications of this fraud all over the country. 
So, the way forward, Madam, is that we have to amend the Stamp Act, 
and, we have to introduce a modern technology for foolproof collection of important 
sources of revenue for the State Gove rnments and the Government is also 
considering how best to play a catalytic role in facilitating a system thereby 
dematerialisation of stamps with computer connectivity can be installed, and, if 
necessary, the Central Government would consider funds for the pilot phase to 
introduce a system which will encourage. 
We are clear, and, I wish to reiterate, though I said so on earlier 
occasions also, that citizens who executed documents on those papers 
373 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2003] 
will not be put to any inconvenience, or, harassment, and, if required, we will 
introduce necessary legislative changes in this regard. 
There is considerable speculation about the extent of fraud. I have said in 
the other House that the seizure of fake stamp papers is about Rs. 3,500 
crores. I wish to, in all honesty, share with the hon. Members that various figures 
are now cited. From Rs. 35,000 crores, Rs. 30,000 crores, Rs. 60,000 crores. 
Please reflect for a moment, that if Rs. 60,000 crores of fake stamp papers were 
in circulation, and, have been utilized, then it would mean that the magnitude of 
the transaction on those stamp papers is over Rs. six lakh crores. It is absolutely 
impossible. It is highly improbable and entirely speculative figure, which really 
results in great deal of needless anxiety being caused in the citizens. There is a 
wrong that has taken place. The wrong must be corrected. The guilty must be 
punished. But, it is necessary that, at l east, in Assemblies, like the Parliament, 
we should be very careful about the figures we cite in regard to this entire 
matter. 
[MR. CHAIRMAN in the Chair] 
The CBI and the Income Tax Authorities are already investigating the 
matter, and, I have said in the other H ouse, that the Inco me Tax Department 
has taken a number of measures, and, some 47 odd properties have been 
seized. The solution to all this to myself lie in handing over the entire matter to the 
Central Bureau of Investigation, and that the future lies in dematerialisation of 
stamp papers, modernisation, and this kind of system that we have in which 
everything has to be on a stamp paper, progressively we have to get away from 
it. But the States, which have individual Stamp Paper Act, have also to reflect on 
this. I do believe, Sir, that this addresses all the significant or major query that 
were raised by the hon. Members in this regard. Thank you.

THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN (DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMAHEPTULLA): I thank 
you, Mr. Chairman, Sir. This is the last day of this Session which was a very 
historic one, very short and very crisp, because we had just a few days due to 
the election results coming out. We always do good business, in spite of all the 
heat and agitation, happiness and anger, which is part of the political and 
democratic life. But, the most important of it is that we celebrated the 200th 
Session of our Rajya Sabha, and we proudly not only lighted our building but also 
had very many celebrations in the Central Hall, by recognising Pranabji who has 
been of great help, throughout, in running this House, honouring him and other old 
Members who have not been here with us, and those who are not in this world also. 
But, I think, the most important event which, I feel, of the 200th Session 
celebrations was the Seminar which we organised—and the Secretariat had 
worked very hard for it—because that Seminar had significance. We always feel 
that there is apathy of the youth towards politics. There were about 100 youth 
who came from the 18 prime institutions of our country, from the Central 
Universities and such other institutions, and listened for almost eight hours to the 
various speeches. They had participated in the debate. I think it is a very good 
effort towards creating an understanding among the youth and trying to make 
them feel a part of our democratic process. I hope that we, in Rajya Sabha, under 
your leadership, will continue this initiative for creating a better understanding about 
the political system of our country and attracting the youth, the cream of our 
society, as it was done during the independence movement, to the political 
governance of this country. 
I thank you, Sir, for your guid ance. I thank the Leader of the O pposition, 
the Leader of the House, the Minister of Parliamentary Affairs, the various leaders 
and the Whips, because we generally forget the Whips. It is the Whips who really 
whip everybody and get the House to run. I also thank the Secretariat and all the 
other Members of Parliament who have been very, very kind and cooperative, in 
spite of very heated arguments
